list: Each term names the process that is rate limiting, meaning the slower one, for what is seen in the plasma; the longer half-life always belongs to it.
Disposition means everything that happens to a drug after it is absorbed, distribution and elimination together, so disposition rate limiting means elimination is the slow step.
Absorption rate limiting is the reverse.

question.stem: For a second drug, the measured rate of elimination is plotted against the plasma concentration at which it was measured, as shown. What does this figure indicate about its elimination?

options.why: The rate is the same at every concentration on the axis, so how much drug is present makes no difference to how fast it leaves. A rate that does not depend on the amount present is the definition of zero order, {{frac:dC|dt}} = −k0.

First order requires the rate to rise with concentration, giving a line that climbs from the origin. Selecting this reads a straight line as first order without checking its direction; a horizontal line is straight and still shows no dependence on concentration at all.

Clearance is the slope of rate against concentration, and the slope here is zero, so clearance is not high but undefined as a single constant. This answer comes from treating the height of the line as the clearance, when it is the steepness that carries it.

options.t: The measurements were taken before steady state
options.why: These axes carry no time, so nothing about them depends on whether steady state was reached. Reaching for this imports a timing concern into a plot whose two variables are a rate and a concentration.

list: Across the figure the concentration rises ninefold, from 2 to 18 mg/L, while the rate of elimination does not move.
The process removing the drug is working at a fixed capacity, so the same amount leaves per hour regardless of how much is there: zero order.
Zero order gives C = C0 − k0t, where k0 is an amount per unit time. The half-life C0/2k0 depends on the starting concentration.
Clearance is the rate of elimination divided by the plasma concentration. With the rate fixed, that ratio falls as concentration rises, so clearance is no longer one number.
On these axes, a line rising from the origin means first order, and its slope is the clearance.

question.stem: A drug eliminated by first-order kinetics is given as the same IV bolus dose at a fixed interval. How long does it take to reach the plateau?

options.why: Elimination is first order, so how close the level is to its plateau is set by how many half-lives have passed. After 3 to 5 half-lives the peaks and troughs have stopped climbing and each dose reaches the same maximum and minimum.

Choosing this counts doses where the rule counts half-lives. With a half-life of 4 hours, 3 to 5 half-lives is 12 to 20 hours: 2 to 3 doses (at 0, 8 and 16 hours) with a dose every 8 hours, but 7 to 11 doses with a dose every 2 hours.

Choosing this treats the first trough as the plateau. One interval brings the level down to the first trough, not to the plateau. The second dose then starts from that trough, and the peaks keep climbing for several more intervals. That climb is accumulation.

options.t: A time that doubles when the dose doubles
options.why: This answer ties the time to plateau to the dose. A first-order rate is proportional to the amount present, so a larger dose is eliminated faster in proportion, and the time to plateau does not change. Doubling the dose doubles the plateau level instead.

teach.t: The plateau is reached when the peaks and troughs stop rising: 3 to 5 half-lives with first-order elimination, whatever the dose.

list: The climb stops when the drug eliminated over one interval equals one dose.
Each half-life closes half of the remaining gap to the plateau: 50 per cent of the way there after one half-life, 75 after two, 87.5 after three and about 97 after five.
Her slide "Drug accumulation with repeated administration" puts it as 3 to 5 half-lives, not 3 to 5 doses.
10 mg/kg every 8 hours, with a half-life of 4 hours and VD (apparent volume of distribution) 0.25 L/kg. Each dose adds C0 = 40 mg/L.
The peaks climb from 40 to 53.3 mg/L and the troughs from 10 to 13.3 mg/L. The climb is over within 3 to 5 half-lives, 12 to 20 hours.

question.stem: A female patient (35 years old, 65 kg) with normal renal function is to be given a drug by IV infusion. According to the literature, the elimination half-life of this drug is 7 hours and the apparent VD is 23.1% of body weight. The pharmacokinetics of this drug assumes a first-order process. The desired steady-state plasma level for this antibiotic is 10 mcg/mL. If the patient suddenly develops partial renal failure, how long would it take for a new steady-state plasma level to be established (assume that 95% of the Css is a reasonable approximation)?

options.why: 95% of Css takes 4.32 half-lives: 0.95 = 1 − e^(−kt) gives t = {{frac:ln 20|k}}. Renal failure lowers clearance and so lengthens the half-life, so the new half-life has to be found first, as her key says.

options.t: About 30.3 hours, as before the renal failure
options.why: Picking this keeps the old half-life. 30.3 hours is 4.32 half-lives of 7 hours; with less clearance k is smaller, the half-life is longer, and the new plateau is reached later.
This counts the right number of half-lives with the wrong half-life. After renal failure k = {{frac:ClT|VD}} falls, so each half-life is longer than 7 hours.

options.t: No time: the level stays at the old steady state
options.why: Picking this treats the plateau as fixed once reached. Css = {{frac:R|ClT}}; when ClT falls at the same rate R, the level rises toward a new, higher plateau, and that climb takes 4.32 of the new half-lives.

teach.h: A change in clearance during an infusion
list: Css = {{frac:R|ClT}}: lower clearance at the same rate gives a higher plateau.
k = {{frac:ClT|VD}}: lower clearance gives a smaller k and a longer half-life.
The time to the new plateau is set by the new half-life: 3 to 5 half-lives, or 4.32 for 95%.

question.quote: One would have to establish the new t½ for the patient, but the time to reach Css would be 4.32 t½ (see part a)

question.stem:
The table below shows the decomposition of a drug as a function of time.

Time (minute) | Drug A (mg)
10 | 97.0
20 | 89.0
40 | 73.0
60 | 57.0
90 | 34.0
120 | 10.0
130 | 2.5

Which order of reaction describes the decrease in the amount of drug A?

options.why: From 20 to 40 minutes the amount falls from 89.0 to 73.0 mg, and from 40 to 60 minutes from 73.0 to 57.0 mg: 16.0 mg lost in each 20 minutes. Equal quantities lost in equal intervals (constant differences, not ratios) is the zero-order signature.

Picking this reads a continuous fall as the first-order signature; first order needs a constant ratio over equal intervals. Over 20 minutes, {{frac:89.0|73.0}} is 1.22 and {{frac:73.0|57.0}} is 1.28; over 30 minutes, {{frac:57.0|34.0}} is 1.68 and {{frac:34.0|10.0}} is 3.40. The ratios climb, so it is not first order.

Choosing this treats the unequal spacing of the time points as a reason the data cannot be classified. Unequal spacing adds arithmetic, not ambiguity: take the difference or ratio over whatever interval separates the points. The two 20-minute pairs, 89.0 to 73.0 mg and 73.0 to 57.0 mg, each lose 16.0 mg: zero order.

list: To decide the order from a data set, compare what happens over equal time intervals.
Equal differences, the same amount lost per interval, mean zero order: C = C0 − kt is a straight line on linear axes.
Equal ratios, the same fraction lost per interval, mean first order: ln C against time is a straight line.
From two points, zero order gives k0 = {{frac:C1 − C2|t2 − t1}}; first order gives k = {{frac:ln(C1 ÷ C2)|t2 − t1}}.
On the exam a data set is supplied and the order has to be decided from it.

question.quote: Zero-order — the drug is decreasing at a constant amount per unit time

question.stem: A drug has a renal clearance well below the clearance that would be expected from glomerular filtration alone. What accounts for this?

options.why: Reabsorption occurs when the renal clearance is less than the calculated clearance by filtration, because drug that was filtered into the lumen moves back into the bloodstream instead of leaving in the urine.

Secretion adds drug to the lumen, so it raises renal clearance above the filtration rate rather than lowering it. Choosing it means applying the right vocabulary to the wrong direction of the inequality, which is the commonest error on this pair.

Picking this changes the reference value instead of naming a process acting on the drug. A higher filtration rate would deliver more drug into the lumen and raise renal clearance, not lower it. Filtered drug returning to the blood, which is reabsorption, explains a value below it.

Picking this answers a kidney question with a liver process: faster metabolism changes hepatic clearance, not renal clearance. Drug reaching the nephron is still filtered, secreted and reabsorbed as before. Only a renal process can move renal clearance below the filtration clearance, and here that process is reabsorption.

list: Secretion and reabsorption are inferred from one comparison: measured renal clearance against the clearance calculated from filtration, the glomerular filtration rate (GFR) of about 120 mL/min.
Above it: drug is being added to the lumen actively, so secretion is present.
Below it: filtered drug is being returned to the blood, so reabsorption is present.
Both are inferences from one measured number set against a known reference value, not direct observations of the process.
Her slide "Tubular Reabsorption" states the comparison.

question.quote: Reabsorption occurs if the renal clearance is less than the calculated clearance by filtration.

question.stem: Which term below describes a comparison of the bioavailability of the active drug in the systemic circulation following extravascular administration with the bioavailability of the same drug following intravenous administration?

options.why: Her slide "Absolute Bioavailability" word for word: extravascular compared with intravenous. The IV dose is the reference because all of it reaches the systemic circulation.
Picking this takes a test between two products for a comparison with IV. Bioequivalence asks whether two products differ significantly in rate and extent of absorption.
Picking this names the release of drug from the product, the step that leads to bioavailability, not a comparison of two routes.
Picking this keeps the comparison but changes the reference. Relative bioavailability compares two extravascular products, such as a tablet against an oral solution, with no IV dose.

Relative: one extravascular product against another, Frel = {{frac:AUCA|AUCB}} × {{frac:DB|DA}}.
